Thomas Kelly
TAH-mus KEL-ee
proper noun
English form of the Greek Thomas (“twin”), joined to the Irish surname Kelly (from Ceallach, “bright-headed” or “contention”); the name of the Dublin hymnwriter who sang the exaltation of Christ.

See also: Thomas Kelly

📖 Biblical Definition

Thomas Kelly (1769–1855), son of an Irish judge and himself trained for the bar, was brought under deep conviction of sin while preparing to defend the law, and finding no peace in the works of the law he was led by grace to rest wholly upon the finished work of Christ. Forsaking his prospects, he took orders, but his evangelical fervour so displeased the Archbishop of Dublin that he was silenced in the establishment; undaunted, he preached in unconsecrated halls and gave the remainder of his long life to the gospel and to sacred song. He composed some seven hundred and sixty-five hymns, of which the noblest exalts the ascended and glorified Redeemer: “The head that once was crowned with thorns is crowned with glory now.” Here Kelly sets the humiliation of Calvary against the coronation of the risen Lord, teaching the church to behold Him who bore the reed and the mocking robe now seated in majesty, “a royal diadem adorns the mighty Victor’s brow.” His hymns breathe the settled joy of a man who had exchanged his own righteousness for Christ’s, and who never wearied of that exchange through fourscore and six years. Generous to the poor of famine-struck Ireland, sound in doctrine, and steadfast in trial, Thomas Kelly is honored as a singer of the crown rights of the exalted Lamb.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Irish hymnwriter (1769–1855), author of “The Head That Once Was Crowned with Thorns.”

expand to see more

THOMAS KELLY, proper noun. Irish evangelical minister and hymnwriter (1769–1855), born in County Queen’s (Laois).

Trained for the law, converted under conviction of sin, and turned to the ministry of the gospel.

Silenced within the established church for his evangelical preaching, he laboured in independent congregations.

Author of some seven hundred and sixty-five hymns exalting the person and finished work of Christ.

Chiefly remembered for “The Head That Once Was Crowned with Thorns,” a hymn of Christ’s exaltation.

📖 Key Scripture

Php 2:9 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:"

Heb 2:9 — "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man."

Rev 19:12 — "His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns; and he had a name written, that no man knew, but he himself."

Mat 27:29 — "And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of the crown rights of the exalted Christ.

expand to see more

This entry is preserved as an honored example, not as the correction of an error. Thomas Kelly’s memory serves to fix the eye of the church upon the ascended Lord and to commend a life laid down for the gospel after every earthly prospect was surrendered for Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exaltation of Christ as the settled ground of the believer’s joy. “The head that once was crowned with thorns is crowned with glory now”—the same Jesus who tasted death for His people now reigns, and the church that beholds His glory is armed against every fear. Let the singing saints look up from the manger and the cross to the throne.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name of the exalted Christ’s singer, from “twin” and the bright Irish house of Kelly.

expand to see more

Thomas — from the Aramaic for “twin,” the apostle’s name borne by many a faithful man.

Kelly — from the Irish Ceallach, an ancient and honorable surname of Erin.

His conversion turned on the law’s inability to justify, driving him to the righteousness of Christ received by faith.

The thorn-crown and the glory-crown supply the great antithesis of his most enduring hymn.

The doctrine of Christ’s ascension and session at God’s right hand shapes the whole of his praise.

Usage

"“Kelly forsook the bar for the pulpit, and the pulpit for the hymnbook of the whole church.”"

"“We closed the service with ‘The head that once was crowned with thorns.’”"

"“His seven hundred hymns all circle back to the exalted Lamb.”"
